opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The tension is real, but people often frame it the wrong way. They assume realism means fidelity to every detail of the real world, and that's both impossible and usually unnecessary. What you need is realism along the axes that matter for the skill you're trying to teach.

So the first question I ask is: what's the behavior we want the model to get better at? If it's navigating a codebase, running tests, and debugging, the environment has to have a real filesystem, real execution, and real error messages. Faking those gives you a model that's good at the fake. But you don't need a full production cluster behind it. A container with the repo and a test harness gets you most of the way. If it's something like customer support or tool use against an API, you often don't need the real backend at all. You need a mock that behaves consistently and returns the kinds of messy, partial, occasionally wrong responses real systems return. That messiness is what's worth preserving.

The second piece is the reward signal. A lot of the "realism" budget should go there rather than into the world itself. If your verifier is sloppy, the model will find the gap and exploit it, and then it doesn't matter how beautiful your simulation is. I'd rather have a fairly simple environment with a tight, hard-to-game check than an elaborate world with a fuzzy grader.

On efficiency, the practical things matter a ton. Make environments cheap to reset. Make them stateless where you can, or snapshot state so you're not rebuilding from scratch every rollout. Keep the action space and the observation format compact, because every extra token in an observation is paid for across thousands of rollouts. And make them parallelizable from day one. If a single episode takes thirty seconds of wall clock because you're waiting on some slow service, that's going to dominate your training throughput way more than the model forward pass.

The approach I like is starting minimal and adding realism only when you see a specific failure. You train, then look at the transcripts. Is the model doing something that would obviously break in the real world but works in the sim? That's a signal to add the missing piece. Is it learning the skill and transferring fine? Then you don't need more fidelity, and adding it just slows everything down.

Diversity probably matters more than depth for any single environment, too. A model that has seen a thousand moderately realistic environments tends to generalize better than one that has seen ten hyper-realistic ones. So a lot of the engineering effort goes into making environments easy to author and compose, so you can get breadth without each one becoming a huge project.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd push back on a little bit is the framing that realism is the goal. Realism is instrumental. What you actually want is transfer — you want the skills the model learns in the environment to show up when it's doing the real task. And it turns out a lot of what makes an environment "realistic" in the sense of being faithful to production doesn't matter for transfer, and a lot of what does matter isn't about realism at all, it's about the structure of the task and the quality of the reward signal.

So the way I tend to think about it is: what are the actual failure modes of the model on the real task? Is it that it doesn't know how to recover when a tool call errors out? Is it that it loses track of state over a long horizon? Is it that it doesn't verify its own work before saying it's done? Those are the things you want to reproduce. And you can often reproduce them in a pretty stripped-down environment. You don't need a full Kubernetes cluster to teach a model that it should check the output of a command before moving on. You need a sandbox where commands sometimes fail in plausible ways and where the reward actually depends on the model noticing.

Where efficiency comes in is mostly about where you spend your compute budget. In RL you're generating a huge number of rollouts, and if every rollout requires spinning up a heavy container and hitting real services, you're going to be bottlenecked on the environment rather than on the model. So there's a lot of value in making environments cheap to reset, cheap to step, and parallelizable. Mocking out the expensive parts, caching what you can, having the environment be mostly deterministic so you can debug it. And honestly, a lot of the engineering work is just making sure the environment doesn't have bugs, because the model will find them. If there's any way to get reward without doing the task, it'll find that way, and now you've trained something you didn't want.

The other piece I think people underrate is verifiability. The environments that work best are the ones where you can check the answer cheaply and reliably. Code with tests, math with a checker, agentic tasks where there's a well-defined end state you can inspect. When you have that, you can afford to be less realistic in other dimensions, because the signal is clean. When you don't have that, and you're relying on an LLM judge or something fuzzier, then every bit of unrealism in the environment becomes a place where the model can exploit the judge, and you have to be a lot more careful.

So I'd say the practical heuristic is: start simple, start cheap, make sure the reward is tight, and then add complexity only when you can point to a specific gap between what the model does in the environment and what it does in the wild. Realism for its own sake tends to just make everything slower without buying you much.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: realistic in what ways? You can spend a lot of compute making a simulation look like the real world without making it a better environment for learning the thing you care about.

For an agent using a computer, for example, you might care much more about whether actions have persistent consequences, whether information is incomplete, and whether the agent has to recover from mistakes than whether every visual detail is perfect. Those are the parts I’d try to preserve. Then I’d simplify everything else as aggressively as I could.

The test is whether the behavior transfers. Does getting better in your simulated environment actually make the agent better at the real task? You want a loop where you train cheaply in simulation, check against real tasks, and use the failures to decide where you need more fidelity. Otherwise, you can end up building a very elaborate world that teaches the wrong lessons.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is figuring out which parts of reality actually matter for the behavior you’re trying to train. You don’t necessarily need a simulation that looks realistic. You need one where the agent has to make the right kinds of decisions, under the right kinds of constraints.

So, for a coding agent, that might mean a real filesystem, a terminal, tests, and dependencies that can break. You probably don’t need to simulate an entire company around it. But if you abstract away every messy detail, you can end up with an agent that’s very good at your environment and not very useful outside it.

I’d start with something simple and cheap, then use failures on real tasks to tell you where to add fidelity. And efficiency matters because it determines how much experimentation you can do. A slightly less realistic environment that lets you run many more useful experiments can be a better tradeoff—as long as you keep checking that improvements transfer.
